solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: What may contain mild defect, nothing more for Spooner? (4,3)

indicatorNotes.for Spooner: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so this asks for that swap

blocks.note: mere = nothing more; it takes the B from the other word
a bug is a defect; it takes the M from the other word

annotation.surface: Someone describes a trivial flaw and asks how Spooner would put it.
annotation.walkthrough: Mild is a dark, low-strength British beer, so the definition is a container for it, not a gentle remark.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by function: mild is a beer, and this is the vessel a pint of it is drunk from.

entries.clue: Pardon received by supreme order (6)

indicatorNotes.received by: one thing received by another is taken inside it

annotation.surface: A pardon granted on the highest authority.
annotation.walkthrough: "Supreme order" reads as one phrase, but the break comes after "supreme".
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, slightly formal: something done at someone's bidding is done on their command.

entries.clue: I will shackle introduction of merchandise but not stop trade (7)

indicatorNotes.will shackle: EGO holds the other letters inside it as a shackle holds a limb
indicatorNotes.introduction of: the introduction of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: the ego is the I, the self

annotation.surface: A trader vows to restrain new goods without halting business altogether.
annotation.walkthrough: "I will" reads as a promise, but I is the ego and "will shackle" is the container. The definition is a verb phrase, so the answer is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb for a government ban: to prohibit commerce with a country is to impose this.

entries.clue: Possibly unable to start a fire without peer (9)

annotation.definition2: Possibly unable to start a fire

blocks.clueFragment: Possibly unable to start a fire
blocks.note: a fire-lighter who has run out of the little sticks you strike

annotation.surface: A would-be fire-starter, stuck without a companion.
annotation.walkthrough: The first sense is a whimsical reading of the word as match + less; "Possibly" flags that it is not a dictionary meaning.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: having no equal, and literally lacking a match to strike.

entries.clue: See red mug on ledge upset after a jerk (2,9)

indicatorNotes.upset: in a down clue, upset turns the word upside down, reading it bottom to top
indicatorNotes.after: the reversed ledge comes after A

blocks.note: gob and mug are both slang for the mouth or face
a window ledge is a sill
a tic is an involuntary jerk

annotation.surface: Someone knocks a mug off a ledge after a sudden twitch and loses their temper.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface mug is a cup falling off a shelf; here it is slang for the mouth. In a down clue "on" means placed above.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom for sudden rage, like a missile launching; seeing red is losing your temper.

entries.clue: Not fed on bananas very much (2,3,2)

indicatorNotes.bananas: bananas means crazy, so the letters go mad

annotation.surface: A remark that someone was not fed on bananas very much as a child.
annotation.walkthrough: "Bananas" looks like the food in the diet; it is the instruction to rearrange FED ON.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom for a limitless amount: "it helped no end" means it helped a great deal.

entries.clue: Once called for a woman, or rather for somebody who listens (3)

indicatorNotes.for somebody who listens: the second meaning only works for a listener, since the word is said like NAY

blocks.note: the French word for born, placed before a married woman's former name
nay = or rather, as in "good, nay, excellent"

annotation.surface: Once a word used of a woman, now one for a listener.
annotation.walkthrough: Née is French for born and precedes a woman's maiden name; it is pronounced like nay.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: the marker of a woman's maiden name, and a sound-alike of nay, meaning or rather.

entries.clue: Lopped branch remains after incineration (5)

indicatorNotes.Lopped: lopping cuts off the top, here the first letter

blocks.note: a branch of an organisation is a member; a limb is also a member

annotation.surface: A cut branch leaves only ashes once burnt.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a lopped tree branch on a bonfire; the branch is a MEMBER, a limb.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a glowing coal is what is left once a fire has burnt down.

entries.clue: Feature of knitted — but not crocheted — garment (7)

annotation.definition2: Feature of knitted — but not crocheted —

blocks.clueFragment: Feature of knitted — but not crocheted —
blocks.note: look at the spelling: kniTTed has two of one letter, croche-Ted only one

annotation.surface: A garment made by knitting rather than crochet.
annotation.walkthrough: The feature is in the spelling, not the fabric: knitted has a double T.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: a man's close-fitting Tudor jacket, and a double T read as two words.

entries.clue: Female soldiers plough Clarkson’s land? (8)

blocks.note: an ard is a primitive plough

annotation.surface: Women soldiers ploughing the fields of a TV presenter's farm.
annotation.walkthrough: Jeremy Clarkson, the car-show presenter, now runs a farm in a TV series, hence the question mark. ARD is an old scratch plough.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Clarkson's Farm is his TV show, so his land is the yard around a farm.

entries.clue: OK to occupy hotel (not much food when sharing a cell) (9)

indicatorNotes.when sharing a cell: the two pieces overlap in one grid square, sharing the T

blocks.note: H is Hotel in the phonetic alphabet
TABLE (food, as in "keeps a good table") with its T shared with A BIT

annotation.surface: A prisoner complains the hotel-like cell is fine but the rations are meagre.
annotation.walkthrough: A BIT and TABLE overlap on one T, one crossword cell, so the grid holds A BI(T)ABLE; "cell" is the prison joke.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a building fit to live in is OK to occupy.

entries.clue: Further to the right, further down (5)

blocks.note: blue is the colour of the UK Conservative party

annotation.walkthrough: In Britain blue is the Conservative colour, so bluer is more right-wing.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: more Tory in politics, and sadder in mood.

entries.clue: What’s laid back and unfeeling taking diamonds off retired woman (5)

blocks.note: as = what, as in "do as I say"

annotation.surface: A relaxed, hard-hearted person stripping jewels from an elderly lady.
annotation.walkthrough: "Laid back" and "retired" look like descriptions of people; both are reversal instructions, one for AS and one for HAR.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: any woman's first name will do, and this is a common one.

entries.clue: Injury-time recovery from one’s side? (9)

blocks.note: injury time is added at the end of a match

annotation.surface: A team pulls back a late goal in stoppage time.
annotation.walkthrough: "One's side" reads as a football team; the definition is the sideways direction.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: sideways, coming from the flank rather than head-on.

entries.clue: Antiques got smashed, didn’t they? (3,8)

annotation.surface: Someone asks for confirmation that the antiques were broken.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is an example: "didn't they?" is itself a tag question, tacked onto the statement before it.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: "didn't they?" is a short question tacked onto a statement.

entries.clue: One badly wants to keep butterfly enclosure (8,6)

indicatorNotes.to keep: one word keeps the other inside it

blocks.note: the ringlet is a brown butterfly

annotation.surface: A collector craving a butterfly house.
annotation.walkthrough: "Enclosure" suggests a pen for the butterfly; it is something enclosed in an envelope.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the letter sent with a CV is enclosed in the envelope, so it is an enclosure.

entries.clue: Testing start for Antonelli, opening out of the pits? (9)

indicatorNotes.start for: the start of a word is its first letter
indicatorNotes.opening: A opens up EX-MINING, splitting it

blocks.note: ex = out of; pits are mines, so mining

annotation.surface: A Formula One driver's trial run as he leaves the pit lane.
annotation.walkthrough: Kimi Antonelli is a Formula One driver, and the pits sound like the pit lane; here they are coal mines.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: inspecting or quizzing someone, as in an exam.

entries.clue: Waiving fine, FA reportedly suspended City (8)

indicatorNotes.Waiving: waiving the F means doing without it
indicatorNotes.reportedly: a report is something said and heard, so the word is taken by its sound

annotation.surface: The Football Association lets a fine go and suspends a club called City.
annotation.walkthrough: FA and City look like football, the Football Association and a club; FA is just letters, and City is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the capital of South Australia.

entries.clue: Edge of pound coin assigned this, originally Latin as agreed? (5,2,7)

annotation.definition: Edge of pound coin assigned this, originally Latin as agreed?

blocks.clueFragment: Edge of pound coin assigned this
blocks.note: the surface pushes a design detail; the setter means the words inscribed around the rim of the British pound
reads as a committee's decision; it hints that the phrase is Latin and sounds like a formal phrase meaning as agreed

annotation.surface: A committee agreed a Latin inscription for the rim of the pound coin.
annotation.walkthrough: The motto, meaning "an ornament and a safeguard", was put on coin edges to deter clipping; "as agreed" plays on it sounding like official Latin.
annotation.definitionFit: The Latin motto lettered on the rim of British pound coins, meaning an ornament and a safeguard.

entries.clue: A delicacy one’s served as a result of being in charge (7)

indicatorNotes.being in: the piece before it is placed in, inside, the word that follows

blocks.note: in someone's charge = in their care

annotation.surface: A person in charge is served caviar as a perk.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is an older spelling of caviar.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: sturgeon roe, the classic luxury food served to guests.

entries.clue: Wearing down hare, say, tortoise finally leads (7)

indicatorNotes.leads: to lead is to go in front, so the letter comes first

blocks.note: "say" admits the hare is only loosely a rodent

annotation.surface: In the fable, the tortoise wears down the hare and takes the lead.
annotation.walkthrough: The tortoise-and-hare fable is decoration; "say" covers the fact that a hare is not strictly a rodent.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, rare: an adjective for what erodes, gnawing slowly away.

entries.clue: Spent summer in St Tropez supporting blind partner? (6)

indicatorNotes.supporting: in a down clue, the supporting word sits underneath

blocks.note: "effing and blinding" pairs the two ways of swearing

annotation.surface: A holiday romance in St Tropez with someone who cannot see.
annotation.walkthrough: "Effing and blinding" is British for swearing, so eff is the partner of blind. "Spent" looks like past tense of spend; here it means exhausted.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: worn out, having lost vigour, as a spent force has.

entries.clue: Numbers following it, odd cult is minding one’s back (9)

indicatorNotes.odd: odd means strange, so the letters are rearranged
indicatorNotes.minding: CULT IS minds, keeps, the other piece inside

blocks.note: anagram fodder, split around the next piece

annotation.surface: An odd cult watches its members' backs.
annotation.walkthrough: Numbers is the book of the Bible that follows this one, so "Numbers following it" defines it; it is not a count.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by position: the third book of the Old Testament, with Numbers coming right after.

entries.clue: It’s criminal taking a newspaper (5)

blocks.note: the pink British business daily, known by its initials with the article in front

annotation.surface: Pinching someone's newspaper is a crime.
annotation.walkthrough: Split the answer as THE FT: the Financial Times is a British newspaper.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: the crime of stealing, and the Financial Times split into two words.

entries.clue: Foul now, unfit for consumption (2-3)

annotation.surface: Food that has turned rotten and inedible.
annotation.walkthrough: "Foul" reads as rotten; it is the snooker foul where the cue ball goes into a pocket after hitting another ball.
annotation.definitionFit: A snooker and billiards term: potting the cue ball off another ball, which is a foul.

entries.clue: How house and home end up empty? (5)

indicatorNotes.end: the end of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: answer the question how they end: in a certain letter, preceded by the article
the last letter of both words

annotation.surface: A question about why a house and home end up bare.
annotation.walkthrough: Answer the question literally: house and home both end IN AN E.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: vacuous, empty of sense or content.

entries.clue: A right puritan disturbed by very bad English (9)

indicatorNotes.disturbed by: PRIG is broken into by VILE

blocks.note: a prig is a self-righteous prude

annotation.surface: A puritan upset by dreadful English.
annotation.walkthrough: "A right puritan" reads as a real prude; "A right" is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a special entitlement or advantage granted to some.

entries.clue: Vegetable, like any other, going individually for a song, it seems (3)

blocks.note: p = penny, a price as cheap as a song
surface padding: admits the price is only a pretence

annotation.surface: A vegetable sold cheaply, one at a time, like any other.
annotation.walkthrough: Any vegetable could be priced "1p ea" (a penny each), which is why the clue says "like any other" and "it seems".
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the small green seed of a pod, as ordinary a vegetable as any.

entries.clue: Complex figure destined to take position beside God (7)

indicatorNotes.beside: RA is placed next to ELECT

blocks.note: as in president-elect, destined for office

annotation.surface: A chosen one about to be seated at God's side.
annotation.walkthrough: "Complex figure" is a figure with a psychological complex named after her, not a complicated shape.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by allusion: the Greek heroine who gave her name to a daughter's complex in psychoanalysis.

entries.clue: Change of ends for rowing crew in late shift (7)

indicatorNotes.Change of ends for: the first and last letters trade places

blocks.note: an eight is a rowing crew

annotation.surface: A rowing crew swaps ends of the boat during a late training session.
annotation.walkthrough: EIGHT IN with its outer E and N swapped. "Late shift" suggests work hours; a shift is also a loose dress.
annotation.definitionFit: A pun on shift: a loose nightdress is a shift worn late at night.
